sessions.final: The descent route shows why parentage, date, registration and foreign nationality must be checked together.

sessions.title: CITIZENSHIP BY REGISTRATION - LISTED CATEGORIES AND EXACT RESIDENCE LOGIC
sessions.before: Registration is not an automatic consequence of marriage, Indian ancestry or possession of an OCI card.
sessions.rejected_after: Registration is not an automatic consequence of marriage, Indian ancestry or possession of an OCI card; institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: Section 5 is discretionary ("may register") and excludes an illegal migrant unless the CAA proviso/Section 6B framework applies.

sessions.title: CITIZENSHIP BY NATURALISATION - THIRD SCHEDULE, WAIVER AND THE CAA MODIFICATION
sessions.before: Section 6 permits the Central Government to grant a certificate to a full-age, capable applicant who is not an illegal migrant and satisfies the Third Schedule.
sessions.rejected_after: The relationship among Citizenship by naturalisation - third Schedule, waiver and the caa modification structures meaningful restraints on public power within Citizenship, but its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: The Central Government may waive all or any Third Schedule conditions for distinguished service to science, philosophy, art, literature, world peace or human progress generally.

sessions.title: CITIZENSHIP BY INCORPORATION OF TERRITORY
sessions.before: The Citizenship (Pondicherry) Order, 1962 is the standard illustration.
sessions.rejected_after: The Citizenship (Pondicherry) Order, 1962 organises Citizenship by incorporation of territory to advance meaningful restraints on public power, but its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: If territory becomes part of India, Section 7 authorises the Central Government, by Gazette order, to specify the persons who become citizens because of their connection with that territory and the date from which citizenship operates.

sessions.title: LOSS OF CITIZENSHIP - RENUNCIATION, TERMINATION AND DEPRIVATION
sessions.before: Renunciation is voluntary declaration; termination follows foreign citizenship; deprivation is a compulsory, category-limited government order.
sessions.rejected_after: The common shorthand "deprivation applies to registered and naturalised citizens" is incomplete because the Act contains express inclusions and exclusions; institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: The common shorthand "deprivation applies to registered and naturalised citizens" is incomplete because the Act contains express inclusions and exclusions.

sessions.title: ASSAM ACCORD, SECTION 6A AND THE NRC CUT-OFF
sessions.before: Section 6A is an Assam-specific route to Indian citizenship: pre-1966 entrants are deemed citizens, the 1966–before-25-March-1971 stream faces detection, registration and ten years without electoral-roll inclusion, and post-cut-off entrants receive no protection.
sessions.rejected_after: Section 6A is an instance of constitutional-statutorily authorised asymmetry: a national citizenship law creates an Assam-specific historical settlement; institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: Section 6A creates an Assam-specific citizenship settlement with differentiated cut-offs, but it confers Indian citizenship rather than any separate Assam citizenship.

sessions.title: IN RE: SECTION 6A (17 OCTOBER 2024) - THE CONTROLLING 4:1 JUDGMENT
sessions.before: Article 29(1) protects the ability of a section of citizens to conserve language, script and culture; the petitioners had not proved that Section 6A itself destroyed that ability.
sessions.rejected_after: Justice Pardiwala accepted that the Assam classification was not unconstitutional when enacted in 1985, but concluded that Section 6A(3) had become manifestly arbitrary with the passage of time because.
sessions.final: Article 29(1) protects the ability of a section of citizens to conserve language, script and culture; the petitioners had not proved that Section 6A itself destroyed that ability.

sessions.title: OCI AND PIO EVOLUTION - DIASPORA CONNECTION WITHOUT CITIZENSHIP
sessions.before: OCI is calibrated diaspora access for a foreign national—not dual citizenship—because notified mobility and socio-economic facilities coexist with no vote, no Indian passport and no claim to citizen-reserved public office.
sessions.rejected_after: OCI is calibrated diaspora access for a foreign national—not dual citizenship—because notified mobility and socio-economic facilities coexist with no vote, no Indian passport and no claim to citizen-reserved public office.
sessions.final: OCI is calibrated diaspora access for a foreign national—not dual citizenship—because notified mobility and socio-economic facilities coexist with no vote, no Indian passport and no claim to citizen-reserved public office.

sessions.title: CITIZENSHIP (AMENDMENT) ACT, 2019 AND RULES 2024 - EXACT OPERATION
sessions.before: That does not transform Aadhaar into universal proof of Indian citizenship.
sessions.rejected_after: Its Section 36 savings clause preserves prior rules, orders and actions so far as consistent, while Section 34 keeps other laws operative; institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: The Immigration and Foreigners Act 2025 preserves consistent prior rules and other laws, so new exemption orders do not themselves confer citizenship.

sessions.title: CAA, ARTICLE 14, SECULARISM AND ASSAM - ARGUMENT TREE, NOT SLOGAN
sessions.before: The CAA debate turns on whether a six-community, three-country and 31-December-2014 facilitation is a reasonable humanitarian classification or an under-inclusive religion-coded preference incompatible with Article 14 and secularism.
sessions.rejected_after: The exam-safe conclusion is neither "obviously valid" nor "already unconstitutional", but that the final answer turns on whether the Court accepts the statutory class as a reasonable remedial classification compatible with equality and secularism.
sessions.final: The CAA's constitutional validity turns on whether its differentiated statutory class is accepted as a reasonable remedial classification compatible with equality and secularism.

sessions.title: CITIZENSHIP PROOF AND DOCUMENT TRAPS
sessions.before: India does not use one universal card that proves every route of citizenship.
sessions.rejected_after: A document may be evidence of a fact relevant to citizenship without itself being citizenship; institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: India does not use one universal card that proves every route of citizenship.

sessions.title: PRELIMS CLOSE-OPTION LABORATORY
sessions.before: Prelims Close-Option Laboratory comprises Articles 5-11, Article 5 and Article 6 as its core connected dimensions.
sessions.rejected_after: Why this earns marks: It uses named Articles, Pradeep Jain, Section 6A and a proportionality-style test, while balancing integration against regional vulnerability.
sessions.final: Citizenship questions require the Constitution, statute and binding judgments to be read together, because no single document proves every route or legal status.

sessions.title: PART III AS AN ARCHITECTURE: RIGHTS, LIMITS, REMEDIES AND SPECIAL CONTROLS
sessions.before: Part III is a constitutional operating system, not a bare catalogue: Articles 12-13 identify bound power and invalid law, Articles 14-30 secure six present rights, Article 32 supplies the remedy, and Articles 31A-35 plus 358-359 control exceptional protection or enforcement.
sessions.rejected_after: Under Fundamental Rights, Article 12, Article 13, Articles 14-30 structure Part iii as an architecture: rights, limits, remedies and special controls to advance meaningful restraints on public power, but its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: Part III combines rights, limits and remedies: Articles 12 and 13 control State action and law, while Article 32 converts protected freedoms into enforceable claims.

sessions.title: BENEFICIARIES, VERTICAL AND HORIZONTAL REACH, POSITIVE AND NEGATIVE DUTIES
sessions.before: Fundamental-right analysis must separate beneficiary from respondent: some guarantees belong only to citizens, many protect every person, and Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24 directly reach specified private conduct while positive duties may require State protection.
sessions.rejected_after: Fundamental-right analysis must separate beneficiary from respondent: some guarantees belong only to citizens, many protect every person, and Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24 directly reach specified private conduct while positive duties may require State protection.
sessions.final: Fundamental-right analysis must separate beneficiary from respondent: some guarantees belong only to citizens, many protect every person, and Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24 directly reach specified private conduct while positive duties may require State protection.

sessions.title: QUALIFIED RIGHTS, REASONABLE RESTRICTIONS AND PROPORTIONALITY
sessions.before: Indian Fundamental Rights are qualified but not defeasible at executive will: every restriction must rest on valid law, fit the exact constitutional ground, pursue a legitimate aim and remain rational, necessary, balanced and procedurally safeguarded.
sessions.rejected_after: Indian Fundamental Rights are qualified but not defeasible at executive will: every restriction must rest on valid law, fit the exact constitutional ground, pursue a legitimate aim and remain rational, necessary, balanced and procedurally safeguarded.
sessions.final: Indian Fundamental Rights are qualified but not defeasible at executive will: every restriction must rest on valid law, fit the exact constitutional ground, pursue a legitimate aim and remain rational, necessary, balanced and procedurally safeguarded.

sessions.title: ARTICLE 12 - THE STATE AND THE INSTRUMENTALITY INQUIRY
sessions.before: Article 12 looks beyond legal form to governmental domination: an entity may be State when its financial, functional and administrative relationship reveals pervasive governmental control, while Article 226 may separately reach a non-State body performing a public duty.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 12 looks beyond legal form to governmental domination: an entity may be State when its financial, functional and administrative relationship reveals pervasive governmental control, while Article 226 may separately reach a non-State body performing a public duty.
sessions.final: Article 12 looks beyond legal form to governmental domination: an entity may be State when its financial, functional and administrative relationship reveals pervasive governmental control, while Article 226 may separately reach a non-State body performing a public duty.

sessions.title: ARTICLE 13 - LAW, JUDICIAL REVIEW AND THE VOIDNESS DOCTRINES
sessions.before: Article 13 converts rights into judicially enforceable limits by defining law broadly and using severability, eclipse and non-waiver, while constitutional amendments are reviewed through Article 368 and the basic-structure boundary.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 13 converts rights into judicially enforceable limits by defining law broadly and using severability, eclipse and non-waiver, while constitutional amendments are reviewed through Article 368 and the basic-structure boundary.
sessions.final: Article 13 converts rights into judicially enforceable limits by defining law broadly and using severability, eclipse and non-waiver, while constitutional amendments are reviewed through Article 368 and the basic-structure boundary.

sessions.title: ARTICLE 14 - TWIN EQUALITY, CLASSIFICATION AND ANTI-ARBITRARINESS
sessions.before: classification tests the structure of differentiation; arbitrariness tests irrational, capricious or disproportionate State power even where a neat class is difficult to identify.
sessions.rejected_after: Arbitrariness tests irrational, capricious or disproportionate State power even where a neat class is difficult to identify; institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: Article 14 combines reasonable-classification review with anti-arbitrariness, so formal differentiation cannot shield irrational, capricious or disproportionate State action.

sessions.title: ARTICLES 15 AND 16 - NON-DISCRIMINATION AND PROTECTIVE DISCRIMINATION
sessions.before: Articles 15(4) and 16(4) are not grudging exceptions to equality.
sessions.rejected_after: Articles 15(4) and 16(4) are not grudging exceptions to equality; institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: Yet they remain enabling powers, not an individual Fundamental Right to demand reservation in every setting.

sessions.title: RESERVATION DOCTRINE: CREAMY LAYER, CEILING, PROMOTION, EFFICIENCY, EWS AND SC SUB-CLASSIFICATION
sessions.before: Reservation is a technique of substantive equality, but its design remains evidence-based, reviewable and attentive to creamy-layer exclusion, representation, promotion conditions, backlog treatment, EWS text and administrative efficiency.
sessions.rejected_after: Reservation is a technique of substantive equality, but its design remains evidence-based, reviewable and attentive to creamy-layer exclusion, representation, promotion conditions, backlog treatment, EWS text and administrative efficiency.
sessions.final: Reservation is a technique of substantive equality, but its design remains evidence-based, reviewable and attentive to creamy-layer exclusion, representation, promotion conditions, backlog treatment, EWS text and administrative efficiency.

sessions.title: ARTICLES 17 AND 18 - ANTI-UNTOUCHABILITY AND ANTI-TITLE GUARANTEES
sessions.before: Articles 17 and 18 attack inherited civic hierarchy horizontally and symbolically: untouchability is abolished and punishable, while titles are prohibited without invalidating military, academic or properly used national distinctions.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 17 and The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 define the institutional architecture of Articles 17 and 18 - anti-untouchability and anti-title guarantees, but article 17 is transformative: it does not merely restrain government classification; it constitutionally abolishes a social hierarchy and requires public enforcement.
sessions.final: Articles 17 and 18 attack inherited civic hierarchy horizontally and symbolically: untouchability is abolished and punishable, while titles are prohibited without invalidating military, academic or properly used national distinctions.

sessions.title: ARTICLE 19 - SIX FREEDOMS AND EXACT RESTRICTION GROUNDS
sessions.before: Article 19 protects six citizen freedoms through clause-specific discipline: the State must identify the exact restriction clause and closed ground, after which reasonableness and proportionality test the means.
sessions.rejected_after: "Offensiveness", administrative convenience or vague hurt sentiment is not an independent Article 19(2) ground; institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: Article 19 protects six citizen freedoms through clause-specific discipline: the State must identify the exact restriction clause and closed ground, after which reasonableness and proportionality test the means.

sessions.title: SPEECH, PRESS, RIGHT TO KNOW AND THE FIRST AMENDMENT SETTLEMENT
sessions.before: State of Madras (1950): circulation is part of speech; the ban failed under the original narrow Article 19(2).
sessions.rejected_after: The right to receive information necessary for democratic choice has been read into Article 19(1)(a); institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: Romesh Thappar protected newspaper circulation under Article 19(1)(a), exposing how the original narrow restriction clause constrained censorship.

sessions.title: SEDITION LINEAGE, BNS SECTION 152 AND SPEECH-INCITEMENT DISCIPLINE
sessions.before: "sedition was simply renamed" is inaccurate; and "all sedition-type criminalisation disappeared" is also inaccurate.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 19(2) defines the institutional architecture of Sedition lineage, bns section 152 and speech-incitement discipline, but the Supreme Court upheld IPC section 124A only by reading it down to speech involving incitement to violence or a tendency/intention to create public disorder.
sessions.final: On 11 May 2022, the Supreme Court placed use of IPC section 124A in abeyance while reconsideration occurred.

sessions.title: DIGITAL SPEECH: SHREYA SINGHAL, INTERNET SHUTDOWNS AND CRIMINAL DEFAMATION
sessions.before: The current criminal provision is BNS section 356, not the repealed IPC sections 499-500.
sessions.rejected_after: Speech under Article 19(1)(a) and trade under Article 19(1)(g), when conducted through the internet, remain constitutionally protected; institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: Digital-speech regulation must reconcile public-order and reputational interests with chilling effects, procedural burdens and the availability of narrower civil remedies.

sessions.title: ARTICLE 20 - EX POST FACTO LAW, DOUBLE JEOPARDY AND SELF-INCRIMINATION
sessions.before: Article 20 creates three person-protective criminal shields against retrospective penal liability, repeated prosecution-and-punishment for the same offence, and compelled testimonial self-incrimination.
sessions.rejected_after: Under Fundamental Rights, Article 20(3) structures Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy and self-incrimination to advance meaningful restraints on public power, but its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: Article 20 restrains criminal power through protections against retrospective penal liability, double jeopardy and compelled testimonial self-incrimination, each operating within its defined scope.

sessions.title: ARTICLE 21 - GOPALAN TO MANEKA: FAIR PROCEDURE AND THE DIGNITY CHARTER
sessions.before: Article 21 became a dignity charter when Maneka Gandhi required fair, just and reasonable procedure and linked liberty with Articles 14 and 19, enabling named protections without turning every policy aspiration into an unlimited entitlement.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 21 protects every person: no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law; institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: Article 21 became a dignity charter when Maneka Gandhi required fair, just and reasonable procedure and linked liberty with Articles 14 and 19, enabling named protections without turning every policy aspiration into an unlimited entitlement.

sessions.title: PRIVACY, PROPORTIONALITY, DNA TESTING AND DATA PROTECTION
sessions.before: 843(E), as of 21 August 2026 the definition and Data Protection Board/institutional provisions specified in the notification are operative.
sessions.rejected_after: truth and identity may justify testing in a strong case; the statutory legitimacy presumption and child's social dignity weigh heavily; less intrusive evidence must be considered; the order must be necessary and proportionate; and refusal consequences cannot be mechanically converted into forced bodily intrusion.
sessions.final: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 section 116 carries the conclusive presumption of legitimacy for a child born during a valid marriage or within 280 days after dissolution while the mother remains unmarried, unless non-access is shown.

sessions.title: ARTICLE 21A - EDUCATION AS A FUNDAMENTAL RIGHT
sessions.before: Article 21A demonstrates a shift from judge-developed Article 21 content to an express, age-bounded Fundamental Right implemented by statute.
sessions.rejected_after: The State shall provide free and compulsory education to children aged six to fourteen in the manner determined by law; institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust protected minority institutions from that application to preserve Article 30(1).

sessions.title: ARTICLE 22 - ORDINARY ARREST, PREVENTIVE DETENTION AND THE UNENFORCED 44TH AMENDMENT CLAUSE
sessions.before: Article 22 separates ordinary arrest from preventive detention: the first carries grounds, counsel and twenty-four-hour production safeguards, while the second follows a distinct regime whose current no-Advisory-Board ceiling remains three months.
sessions.rejected_after: Preventive detention is the rights chapter's deepest structural contradiction: it constitutionalises detention without trial, yet surrounds it with minimum review, communication and representation safeguards.
sessions.final: Article 22 separates ordinary arrest from preventive detention: the first carries grounds, counsel and twenty-four-hour production safeguards, while the second follows a distinct regime whose current no-Advisory-Board ceiling remains three months.

sessions.title: ARTICLES 23-24 - EXPLOITATION, FORCED LABOUR AND CHILD LABOUR
sessions.before: Article 24's text is narrower than a complete ban on every kind of child work, while the amended statute creates broader prohibitions and defined exceptions.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 24's text is narrower than a complete ban on every kind of child work,; institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: Article 24's text is narrower than a complete ban on every kind of child work, while the amended statute creates broader prohibitions and defined exceptions.

sessions.title: ARTICLES 25-28 - CONSCIENCE, DENOMINATION, SECULAR REGULATION AND PRINCIPLED DISTANCE
sessions.before: Indian religious freedom protects conscience and denominational autonomy while permitting public-order, health, morality, secular-regulation and social-reform controls; the governing model is principled distance, not either theocracy or an absolute wall.
sessions.rejected_after: Indian religious freedom protects conscience and denominational autonomy while permitting public-order, health, morality, secular-regulation and social-reform controls; the governing model is principled distance, not either theocracy or an absolute wall.
sessions.final: Indian religious freedom protects conscience and denominational autonomy while permitting public-order, health, morality, secular-regulation and social-reform controls; the governing model is principled distance, not either theocracy or an absolute wall.

sessions.title: ARTICLES 29-30 - CULTURAL CONSERVATION AND MINORITY EDUCATIONAL AUTONOMY
sessions.before: Articles 29-30 protect cultural conservation, non-discriminatory admission and minority educational autonomy, but Article 29 is not minority-exclusive and Article 30 protects administration rather than maladministration.
sessions.rejected_after: Articles 29-30 protect cultural conservation, non-discriminatory admission and minority educational autonomy, but Article 29 is not minority-exclusive and Article 30 protects administration rather than maladministration.
sessions.final: Articles 29-30 protect cultural conservation, non-discriminatory admission and minority educational autonomy, but Article 29 is not minority-exclusive and Article 30 protects administration rather than maladministration.

sessions.title: ARTICLE 32 AND THE FIVE WRITS
sessions.before: Article 32 makes the Supreme Court a guaranteed Fundamental-Rights forum, while Article 226 is wider in subject matter and public-duty reach; the correct writ follows the defect—detention, unperformed duty, threatened excess, defective order or unlawful public office.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 32 makes the Supreme Court a guaranteed Fundamental-Rights forum, while Article 226 is wider in subject matter and public-duty reach; the correct writ follows the defect—detention, unperformed duty, threatened excess, defective order or unlawful public office.
sessions.final: Article 32 makes the Supreme Court a guaranteed Fundamental-Rights forum, while Article 226 is wider in subject matter and public-duty reach; the correct writ follows the defect—detention, unperformed duty, threatened excess, defective order or unlawful public office.

sessions.title: ARTICLES 31A, 31B AND 31C - SAVING PROVISIONS WITHOUT BLANKET IMMUNITY
sessions.before: Articles 31A-31C, 33-35 create defined constitutional controls rather than rights-free zones: their field, purpose and legislative competence remain text-bound and subject to basic-structure review where applicable.
sessions.rejected_after: Articles 31A-31C, 33-35 create defined constitutional controls rather than rights-free zones: their field, purpose and legislative competence remain text-bound and subject to basic-structure review where applicable.
sessions.final: Articles 31A-31C, 33-35 create defined constitutional controls rather than rights-free zones: their field, purpose and legislative competence remain text-bound and subject to basic-structure review where applicable.

sessions.title: RIGHT TO PROPERTY: ARTICLE 31 TRANSITION TO ARTICLE 300A
sessions.before: Article 300A is a constitutional right, though not a Fundamental Right.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 300A is a constitutional right, though not a Fundamental Right; institutionally, this supports meaningful restraints on public power, while its protection remains subject to the Constitution's express scope, reasonable qualifications and judicial review.
sessions.final: Article 300A protects property as a constitutional right outside Part III, requiring authority of law even though deprivation no longer directly invokes a Fundamental Right.

sessions.title: ARTICLES 33-35 AND MARTIAL LAW
sessions.before: Martial law does not automatically erase habeas corpus or create unlimited military power.
sessions.rejected_after: Martial law does not automatically erase habeas corpus or create unlimited military power.
sessions.final: Martial law does not automatically erase habeas corpus or create unlimited military power.

sessions.title: ARTICLES 358 AND 359 - TWO DIFFERENT EMERGENCY MECHANISMS
sessions.before: Article 358 automatically displaces Article 19 constraints only during war or external-aggression Emergency within its conditions, whereas Article 359 requires a Presidential order suspending court enforcement of specified rights and can never include Articles 20 or 21.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 358 automatically displaces Article 19 constraints only during war or external-aggression Emergency within its conditions, whereas Article 359 requires a Presidential order suspending court enforcement of specified rights and can never include Articles 20 or 21.
sessions.final: Article 358 automatically displaces Article 19 constraints only during war or external-aggression Emergency within its conditions, whereas Article 359 requires a Presidential order suspending court enforcement of specified rights and can never include Articles 20 or 21.

sessions.title: ARTICLE 359: THE NON-DEROGABLE ARTICLES 20 AND 21 CORE
sessions.before: Current Part III analysis must be date-bounded: Electoral Bonds protects political-funding information, Davinder Singh permits evidence-based Scheduled Caste sub-classification, Property Owners preserves original Article 31C, DPDP commencement is phased, and BNS section 152 remains under a notified constitutional challenge without a located final merits decision.
sessions.rejected_after: Articles 19(1)(d) and 19(1)(e) make internal mobility and settlement core incidents of common citizenship, but Article 19(5) expressly subjects both to reasonable restrictions.
sessions.final: Article 359 may suspend specified enforcement remedies during an Emergency but cannot suspend Articles 20 and 21, preserving a non-derogable constitutional core.

sessions.title: PART IV AS CONSTITUTIONAL ARCHITECTURE
sessions.before: This common definition links Parts III and IV: the same public power restrained by Fundamental Rights is directed toward welfare ends by Part IV.
sessions.rejected_after: This common definition links Parts III and IV: the same public power restrained by Fundamental Rights is directed toward welfare ends by Part IV.
sessions.final: Part IV directs the same State restrained by Fundamental Rights toward welfare goals, linking limited government with social transformation.

sessions.title: ARTICLE 37: NON-JUSTICIABILITY, DUTY AND POLITICAL SANCTION
sessions.before: It is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 37 converts flexibility into responsibility by retaining a constitutional duty and electoral sanction; institutionally, this supports accountable governance, while its practical authority remains subject to constitutional text, institutional competence and reviewable procedure.
sessions.final: Article 37 makes Directive Principles non-justiciable but fundamental in governance, converting them from enforceable claims into legislative duties and political standards.

sessions.title: COMPLETE ARTICLE-BY-ARTICLE COVERAGE: ARTICLES 38 TO 43B
sessions.before: Articles 38 to 43B convert the Constitution's welfare commitment into linked directives on distributive justice, access to justice, local self-government, labour dignity, social security and democratic economic organisation.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 39(b) and Article 39(c) organise Complete Article-by-Article coverage: articles 38 to 43b to advance accountable governance, but its practical authority remains subject to constitutional text, institutional competence and reviewable procedure.
sessions.final: Articles 38 to 43B convert the Constitution's welfare commitment into linked directives on distributive justice, access to justice, local self-government, labour dignity, social security and democratic economic organisation.

sessions.title: COMPLETE ARTICLE-BY-ARTICLE COVERAGE: ARTICLES 44 TO 51
sessions.before: Articles 44 to 51 widen the Directive Principles beyond material welfare by constitutionalising reform, capability, ecology, heritage, judicial independence and a peace-oriented international outlook.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 49, Article 51 and Article 46 define the institutional architecture of Complete Article-by-Article coverage: articles 44 to 51, but article 41 expressly depends on economic capacity and development.
sessions.final: Article 49 is not a generic culture clause; it protects nationally important monuments, places and objects within the Parliamentary-law framework.

sessions.title: CLASSIFICATION: USEFUL SCHOLARSHIP, NOT CONSTITUTIONAL TEXT
sessions.before: Article 43 is socialistic for living wage and Gandhian for rural cottage industries.
sessions.rejected_after: The familiar division is a scholarly/Laxmikanth classification based on content and direction; institutionally, this supports accountable governance, while its practical authority remains subject to constitutional text, institutional competence and reviewable procedure.
sessions.final: The socialistic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual grouping aids revision, but overlapping provisions show that it is scholarly classification rather than constitutional text.

sessions.title: AMENDMENTS THAT CHANGED PART IV
sessions.before: Part IXB invalid/inoperative for State co-operative societies; Part IXB operative for multi-State co-operative societies; Article 43B and the amendment to Article 19(1)(c) were not struck down.
sessions.rejected_after: The case demonstrates that implementing a DPSP cannot bypass federal amendment procedure.
sessions.final: The 97th Amendment's Part IXB altered that State legislative field without the ratification required by the proviso to Article 368(2).

sessions.title: FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS-DPSP CHRONOLOGY: CONFLICT TO HARMONY
sessions.before: Do not write: "Fundamental Rights always prevail over DPSP." Write: "Enforceable rights retain primacy in ordinary conflict, but constitutional harmony, permissible amendment and the narrow Article 31C shield qualify any absolute hierarchy.".
sessions.rejected_after: Parliament may amend rights and legislate to implement Part IV, but the basic structure - including judicial review and harmony between Parts III and IV - limits that power.
sessions.final: Parliament may amend rights and legislate to implement Part IV, but the basic structure - including judicial review and harmony between Parts III and IV - limits that power.

sessions.title: ARTICLE 31C AFTER PROPERTY OWNERS ASSOCIATION
sessions.before: Article 31C is not a general licence for nationalisation, arbitrary redistribution or immunity from every Fundamental Right.
sessions.rejected_after: Its surviving textual shield is tied to Articles 39(b)/(c) and Articles 14/19; institutionally, this supports accountable governance, while its practical authority remains subject to constitutional text, institutional competence and reviewable procedure.
sessions.final: Article 31C protects laws genuinely implementing Article 39(b) or (c) from Articles 14 and 19 challenges, but basic-structure review prevents unlimited insulation.

sessions.title: FROM DIRECTIVE TO ENFORCEABLE ENTITLEMENT
sessions.before: This is constitutional conversion by mediation, not automatic enforceability: directive - rights interpretation - amendment/statute - institution - remedy and accountability.
sessions.rejected_after: This is constitutional conversion by mediation, not automatic enforceability: directive - rights interpretation - amendment/statute - institution - remedy and accountability.
sessions.final: Unni Krishnan read education up to age 14 into Article 21, subject to the State's capacity beyond that stage.

sessions.title: IMPLEMENTATION MAP: LAW, INSTITUTION, OUTCOME AND HONEST LIMITS
sessions.before: Implementation map: law, institution, outcome and honest limits comprises Implementation map, law and institution as its core connected dimensions.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 51A and Part IV define the institutional architecture of Implementation map: law, institution, outcome and honest limits, but targeted schemes can improve access but may fragment entitlements or create exclusion errors.
sessions.final: Implementation map: law, institution, outcome and honest limits comprises Implementation map, law and institution as its core connected dimensions.

sessions.title: ARTICLE 39A, FREE LEGAL AID AND NALSA
sessions.before: Article 39A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment to secure equal justice and free legal aid so justice is not denied by economic or other disabilities.
sessions.rejected_after: Article 39A, Article 21 and Article 23 define the institutional architecture of Article 39a, free legal aid and nalsa, but section 13 also requires the concerned authority to be satisfied that the applicant has a prima facie case to prosecute or defend.
sessions.final: Article 39A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment to secure equal justice and free legal aid so justice is not denied by economic or other disabilities.

sessions.title: ORDINARY AND PERMANENT LOK ADALATS
sessions.before: If settlement fails, a pending case returns to the referring court at the stage already reached; pre-litigation parties are advised to pursue ordinary remedies.
sessions.rejected_after: Because an ordinary award is founded on settlement, absence of genuine consent attacks the foundation; the Act does not convert a failed conciliation into adjudication.
sessions.final: Because an ordinary award is founded on settlement, absence of genuine consent attacks the foundation; the Act does not convert a failed conciliation into adjudication.

sessions.title: ARTICLE 44 AND THE UNIFORM CIVIL CODE

sessions.rejected_after: A pre-Constitution law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights is generally not erased from the statute book; institutionally, this supports structured adjudication and constitutional control of public power, while judicial application must remain anchored in constitutional text, binding precedent and institutional competence.
sessions.final: The doctrine of eclipse suspends enforcement of an inconsistent pre-Constitution law to the extent of conflict, but does not ordinarily repeal the law.
